title: Labor Law § 740 — Retaliatory action by employers; prohibition (Whistleblower Law)
text: RULE SUMMARY (verbatim text to be backfilled from source URL). New York Labor Law § 740, substantially expanded by 2021 amendments effective January 26, 2022, prohibits an employer from taking any retaliatory action against an employee because the employee discloses, threatens to disclose, or objects to or refuses to participate in an activity, policy, or practice that the employee reasonably believes is in violation of law, rule, or regulation, or that the employee reasonably believes poses a substantial and specific danger to the public health or safety. The 2022 amendments broadened coverage to former employees and independent contractors, replaced the prior 'actual violation' standard with a 'reasonable belief' standard, expanded the definition of retaliatory action to include adverse employment actions and threats, and extended the statute of limitations to two years. Remedies include injunctive relief, reinstatement, back pay, civil penalties, and attorneys' fees. The employee must generally make a good-faith effort to notify the employer before public disclosure, subject to exceptions.

title: Executive Law § 296 — Unlawful discriminatory practices (NY State Human Rights Law)
text: RULE SUMMARY (verbatim text to be backfilled from source URL). Executive Law § 296, the operative provision of the New York State Human Rights Law, makes it an unlawful discriminatory practice for an employer to discriminate against an individual in compensation or in terms, conditions, or privileges of employment because of a protected characteristic, including sex. Subdivision 1(e) and subdivision 7 prohibit retaliation: it is unlawful to retaliate or discriminate against any person because he or she has opposed any practices forbidden under the article or because he or she has filed a complaint, testified, or assisted in any proceeding. Following 2019 amendments, the NYSHRL is construed liberally, the 'severe or pervasive' standard for harassment was eliminated in favor of a lower threshold (conduct that rises above 'petty slights or trivial inconveniences'), and the statute reaches employers of all sizes. Prevailing plaintiffs may recover compensatory damages, punitive damages, and attorneys' fees.

title: NYC Administrative Code § 8-107 — Unlawful discriminatory practices (NYC Human Rights Law)
text: RULE SUMMARY (verbatim text to be backfilled from source URL). The New York City Human Rights Law, codified at Administrative Code § 8-107, is among the most protective anti-discrimination statutes in the country and must be construed independently of and more liberally than its state and federal counterparts (Local Civil Rights Restoration Act of 2005; Williams v. N.Y.C. Housing Auth.). Section 8-107(7) prohibits retaliation against any person for opposing discriminatory practices; the retaliation need only be reasonably likely to deter a person from engaging in protected activity, a standard more protective than Title VII. Harassment need not be 'severe or pervasive' (Mihalik v. Credit Agricole). Remedies include uncapped compensatory and punitive damages and attorneys' fees.

title: Labor Law §§ 191, 193, 198 — Frequency of wage payments; deductions; remedies
text: RULE SUMMARY (verbatim text to be backfilled from source URL). Labor Law § 191 governs the frequency and timing of wage payments, including the requirement to pay wages owed upon termination not later than the regular payday for the pay period worked. Labor Law § 193 prohibits unauthorized deductions from wages. Labor Law § 198 provides the remedial scheme: an employee who prevails on a wage claim is entitled to the full amount of underpaid wages, prejudgment interest, liquidated damages equal to one hundred percent of the wages owed (unless the employer proves a good-faith basis), and reasonable attorneys' fees. Accrued and unused vacation/PTO is payable on separation where the employer's policy or practice treats it as earned wages (12 NYCRR 142-2.16; Glenville Gage).

title: General Obligations Law § 7-103 — Money deposited as security; held in trust
text: RULE SUMMARY (verbatim text to be backfilled from source URL). General Obligations Law § 7-103 provides that whenever money is deposited as security for performance of a lease of real property, that money continues to be the property of the person making the deposit and is held in trust by the landlord; it is not to be mingled with the landlord's personal funds and may not be converted to the landlord's own use. For buildings with six or more dwelling units, the deposit must be placed in an interest-bearing account. Commingling the deposit with the landlord's own funds is a conversion that entitles the tenant to immediate return of the deposit, and the landlord forfeits any right to retain any portion of it even for legitimate damages (Tappan Golf Drive Range v. Tappan Property; LeRoy v. Sayers).

title: General Obligations Law § 7-108 — Returning security deposits (HSTPA 2019)
text: RULE SUMMARY (verbatim text to be backfilled from source URL). General Obligations Law § 7-108, enacted as part of the Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019, governs the return of residential security deposits. The landlord must return the deposit, less any lawful deductions, within fourteen days after the tenant vacates. If the landlord intends to retain any portion for damages beyond ordinary wear and tear, the landlord must provide the tenant an itemized statement of the basis for the amount retained. Critically, if the landlord fails to provide the itemized statement and return the balance within fourteen days, the landlord forfeits any right to retain any portion of the deposit. The landlord bears the burden of proving the reasonableness of any amount withheld. The statute also entitles tenants to an inspection before and after the tenancy.

title: General Business Law § 349 — Deceptive acts and practices unlawful
text: RULE SUMMARY (verbatim text to be backfilled from source URL). General Business Law § 349 declares unlawful deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any business, trade, or commerce in New York. To state a private claim a plaintiff must allege (1) consumer-oriented conduct that is (2) materially misleading and that (3) caused injury (Stutman v. Chemical Bank; Oswego Laborers' Local 214 Pension Fund v. Marine Midland Bank). The deception is measured by an objective 'reasonable consumer acting reasonably under the circumstances' standard. Successful plaintiffs may recover actual damages, statutory damages up to fifty dollars (trebled up to one thousand dollars for willful or knowing violations), and reasonable attorneys' fees in the court's discretion.

title: Real Property Law § 235-b — Warranty of habitability
text: RULE SUMMARY (verbatim text to be backfilled from source URL). Real Property Law § 235-b implies in every residential lease a warranty that the premises are fit for human habitation, fit for the uses reasonably intended by the parties, and that the occupants will not be subjected to conditions dangerous to life, health, or safety. The warranty cannot be waived by any provision in the lease. It applies regardless of the lease's express terms and covers conditions in the dwelling and the common areas. The measure of damages for breach is the difference between the rent reserved under the lease and the reduced rental value of the premises in their defective condition during the period of the breach (Park West Management Corp. v. Mitchell, 47 N.Y.2d 316 (1979)).
